strengths: AugSub offers a simple, technically coherent training modification: a standard supervised pass guides a more strongly regularized pass through shared parameters and a detached prediction target. It adds no parameters or inference cost and accommodates dropout, stochastic depth, and masking.

The main accuracy gains have credible support. Table 3 reports improvements of 0.6–0.7 percentage points across four ViT sizes after 400 epochs. Three-run results in Table A.2 strengthen this evidence; ViT-B improves from 83.46±0.04 to 84.08±0.02.

The paper meaningfully addresses additional computation. In Table 6, ViT-B with AugMask reaches 84.1% using 25 GPU-days, versus 83.7% using 26 GPU-days for longer baseline training. These comparisons support practical value beyond simply spending more compute.

Evaluation covers substantially different architectures and training settings, including ResNet, Swin, MAE/BEiT/CLIP finetuning, robustness, and downstream tasks. For example, ViT-B ImageNet-A accuracy rises from 36.8% to 41.9%, and ADE20K single-scale mIoU improves from 48.8 to 49.4.

The equations, pseudocode, and detailed recipes in Appendix B support reproducibility. Using the same 50% masking ratio across many settings also supports ease of adoption. Overall, the demonstrated usefulness and empirical support favor acceptance despite the attribution and novelty reservations below.
weaknesses: Originality is incompletely established relative to closely related self-distillation and sub-model consistency methods. Co-sub is explicitly acknowledged but receives no experimental comparison. Supporting several drop operators demonstrates flexibility, but does not establish the claimed advance over this closely related approach.

The central loss design lacks decisive controls. Table 1 compares supervised training on corrupted inputs against a method that additionally retains a fully observed supervised pass. A baseline combining supervised losses on both full and corrupted inputs is missing, so the benefit specifically attributable to relaxed targets remains unclear. The contribution of stop-gradient is also not ablated.

The proposed mechanism is overstated. Section 3.1 claims regularization applies exclusively to successfully classified examples, but Equation 3 contains no correctness gate: its student-logit gradient depends on disagreement between predictions, including when the main prediction is wrong. Figure 3 shows aggregate temporal behavior and cannot establish the claimed example-level selectivity. This limits the explanation rather than making the objective ill-defined.

Generality has concrete limits. Table A.3 shows that adding AugMask during ViT-B finetuning reduces CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.89% to 89.55%. Section 4.2 also acknowledges that CLIP's best checkpoint accuracy is unchanged. These results qualify claims of consistently improved finetuning without recipe-specific adjustment.

Statistical support is uneven: several smaller improvements, including BEiT v2's 0.1-point gains and COCO's 0.2/0.3 AP gains, lack repeated-run uncertainty estimates. Their reliability is less established than the main ViT results. Practical benefits also depend on the setting because training costs increase approximately 1.5-fold for token-dropping AugMask and twofold for hierarchical architectures.
